stimuli.title: A speech by a library trustee to a city council, 1876 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Gentlemen of the council, you have asked me to speak briefly, and I will try to honor the request, though the subject tempts a man to speak at length. You are asked tonight to spend the public money on a free library. I know the objection before it is raised. A library, it is said, is a luxury for the idle, and this is a city of workers who have no time to read.

Consider who those workers are. The young man at the foundry who learned his trade by watching another man's hands may one day wish to know why the iron behaves as it does. The clerk who copies letters all day may wish to write one of his own that is worth copying. The mother who cannot afford a single book on the care of children is not idle; she is busier than any of us. It is precisely because these citizens have little time and less money that a free library is no luxury for them. The rich man has his own shelves. The poor man has only ours.

Some of you have said that the saloon and the street corner will always draw more men than any reading room. Perhaps they will. But I have never heard it argued that because some men will drink, no man should be offered water. Open the doors, light the lamps until ten o'clock, and let us see whom we draw.

I will not pretend that books make men good. I have known well-read scoundrels, and so have you. A library makes no promise about character. It promises only that a citizen who wishes to improve himself will not be turned away for want of the price of a book. In a republic that asks every man to judge the questions of the day at the ballot box, that seems a modest promise and a prudent one.

The plan has been laid before you: a rented hall, a librarian, a few thousand volumes to begin. You spend more each year on the paving of streets, and you do so because a city cannot do its business on roads of mud. I ask you only to pave one road more.

stimuli.title: An essay by an urban planner, 2019 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Walk through the center of almost any American city and count the places where you could sit down without buying something. In many downtowns the number is small and shrinking. Benches have been removed from bus stops, ledges have been fitted with metal studs, and the few seats that remain are often divided by armrests placed so that no one can lie down. Each of these choices was made for a reason, usually a complaint. Together they have produced streets that quietly tell a large share of the public to keep moving.

The people most affected are not the ones the changes were aimed at. An older man who walks to the pharmacy needs to rest halfway there. A woman eight months pregnant waits twenty minutes for a bus. A child with a sprained ankle, a delivery worker on a break, a tourist reading a map: all of them use a bench in the way a bench is meant to be used. When a city removes seating to discourage one kind of visitor, it discourages every kind.

Planners have known this for decades. Researchers who filmed public plazas found that the most successful ones, the places people chose to linger, had one feature in common: plenty of places to sit, preferably seats that people could move. A plaza with nowhere to sit stood empty at lunchtime while a plainer one across the street filled up. People attract people, and seating is what keeps them long enough to attract anyone.

None of this means that complaints about benches are imaginary. Seating that is never cleaned or repaired becomes a nuisance, and a bench in the wrong spot can block a doorway. But the answer to a poorly managed bench is a well-managed one, not an empty sidewalk. Cities that have added seating and paid for its upkeep report busier streets, and busy streets are, by most measures, safer ones.

A bench costs less than almost anything else a city builds. It asks nothing of the person who uses it. It may be the most democratic piece of furniture we have, and we should stop treating it as a problem to be solved.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: street trees (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) On a July afternoon, a group of volunteers in our city carried thermometers along two streets a few blocks apart. (2) One street was lined with mature oak trees, and the other had almost none. (3) The sidewalk on the treeless street was more than twenty degrees hotter.

(4) Results like these say something about trees. (5) Shade lowers the temperature of pavement and of the air above it, which matters most during heat waves. (6) Heat kills more people in the United States in a typical year than any other kind of weather. (7) Trees also soak up rainwater, reducing the flooding that overwhelms storm drains after heavy storms.

(8) Some residents worry that tree roots will crack sidewalks. (9) This concern is reasonable. (10) Choosing smaller species and wider planting strips can prevent most of that damage.

(11) The neighborhoods with the fewest trees are often the ones whose residents can least afford air conditioning. (12) A citywide planting program would help out with things for the people who need it most. (13) Planting trees is good.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: small museums online (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) The county historical museum in my town owns more than forty thousand objects, from quilts to farm tools to letters written during the Civil War. (2) On any given day, fewer than a thousand of them are on display. (3) The rest sit in boxes in a basement storeroom that few people have ever seen.

(4) Small museums like this one should photograph their collections and put the images online. (5) A student writing a report on local history could study the letters without traveling to the museum. (6) Families researching their ancestors could find a great-grandmother's quilt. (7) Researchers at universities, who rarely visit small museums, could discover objects that change what we know about the past.

(8) Digitizing a collection is not free. (9) It takes cameras, storage, and staff time a small museum may have only one paid employee. (10) Many states offer grants for this kind of work, and college students often volunteer to help in exchange for experience.

(11) A museum that keeps its collection in the basement protects the objects. (12) But protection is only half of a museum's job. (13) The other half is sharing, and sharing is important.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: apprenticeships (practice text)
stimuli.text: (1) When I told my teachers that I planned to become an electrician, several of them looked disappointed. (2) They assumed that a student with good grades should go to a four-year college. (3) But an apprenticeship let me earn a wage while I learned, and I finished my training with no debt. (4) Electricians are needed everywhere, and the work requires real knowledge of math and physics. (5) Schools should present apprenticeships as an equal choice, not a fallback. (6) Counselors could invite tradespeople to career days, and teachers could stop treating college as the only measure of success. (7) The country needs well-trained workers in the trades, and many students would choose that path if they knew it was respected.

stimuli.title: A commencement address by a physician, 1912 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Graduates, I was asked to give you advice, and I have little to give except one piece I learned by failing to follow it. You have spent four years being rewarded for right answers. The world you are entering will reward you, in the long run, for something else: for noticing when your answers are wrong.

When I was a young doctor I treated a farmer for a fever that would not break. I was sure of my diagnosis. I had read the books, and the books agreed with me. For a week I gave him the medicine the books prescribed, and for a week he grew worse. It was his wife, who had no schooling beyond the village school, who pointed out that the fever rose every evening after he drank from a certain well. I had looked at his chart a hundred times. She had looked at him.

I tell this story not to make myself humble before you, though humility would do me no harm, but because it holds the whole of what I know about my profession. The great danger to a physician is not ignorance. Ignorance can be cured with study. The great danger is certainty, which closes the eyes just when they most need to be open.

You will be tempted, as I was, to defend your first judgment because it is yours. You will be tempted to treat a person who questions you as an enemy of your dignity. Resist. The farmer's wife was no enemy of mine; she was the best colleague I had that year. Every field you enter, whether it is law or teaching or business or the care of the sick, is full of such colleagues, and most of them will not have diplomas.

So I will not wish you success, which will come or not as it pleases. I will wish you the courage to say, more often than you would like, 'I was wrong.' It is the hardest sentence in the language, and the most useful.

stimuli.title: An essay by a former newspaper editor, 2021 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
For eleven years I ran the corrections column of a midsize daily newspaper. It was the least read part of the paper and, I came to believe, the most important. Every correction we printed admitted that we had gotten something wrong: a name misspelled, a date confused, a quotation credited to the wrong council member. Some of my colleagues thought the column made us look careless. I thought it was the clearest evidence we had that we were careful.

The reasoning is simple, though it runs against instinct. Every newspaper makes mistakes, because every newspaper is written quickly by people. A paper that never prints a correction has not avoided error; it has avoided admitting it. Readers are not fools. They notice the misspelled name of their own street. If they never see us fix it, they conclude that we do not care, or worse, that we do not check.

Surveys of news audiences point the same way. Readers who see a clear, prompt correction tend to rate the outlet as more trustworthy, not less. What damages trust is the quiet fix: the online story changed overnight with no note, so that a reader who saw the error the day before now wonders whether she imagined it.

I do not want to romanticize the column. Some corrections were embarrassing, and a few pointed to failures of reporting that should have been caught long before print. A correction is not a substitute for getting it right. But the choice a newsroom faces is not between perfection and error. It is between error that is acknowledged and error that is hidden.

When I left the paper, a reader sent me a note. She had read the corrections column every morning for years, she wrote, because it was the only part of the paper that told her exactly what we had not known the day before. I keep the note on my desk.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: public drinking fountains (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) A century ago, most American parks had public drinking fountains, and many downtown streets did too. (2) Over the decades, as bottled water became common and repairs went undone, many of those fountains were capped or removed. (3) Today a person who gets thirsty in our downtown has two choices: buy a drink or go without.

(4) The loss is not only a matter of convenience. (5) People who work outdoors, such as delivery riders and street vendors, can spend hours in the summer sun. (6) Children playing in parks need water more often than adults realize. (7) Older adults are especially at risk of dehydration, because the sense of thirst weakens with age.

(8) Modern fountains are not the rusty spouts many people remember. (9) Many include a bottle filler and a lower spout for children and wheelchair users. (10) Their water comes from the same public supply, tested to the same standards, as the water in our homes. (11) Some cities report that a single bottle filler in a busy park is used thousands of times a month.

(12) Our city is renovating three downtown parks next spring. (13) Adding fountains during construction is far easier than adding them later. (14) The parks department should include them.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: a repair cafe at the library (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) Last spring, a toaster, a lamp, and a pair of jeans arrived at our town library on the same Saturday morning. (2) None of them was there to be borrowed. (3) They had come to the library's first repair cafe, where volunteers with tools and sewing machines spent four hours fixing whatever neighbors carried in.

(4) By noon the volunteers had repaired thirty-one items. (5) Most would otherwise have been thrown away. (6) Repair cafes began in the Netherlands in 2009 and have since spread to thousands of communities. (7) They work because many broken things need only a small fix; a loose wire, a worn belt, a missing button.

(8) Our town should hold a repair cafe every month. (9) Each repaired item is one less thing in the landfill and one less purchase for a family on a tight budget. (10) Repair cafes also do something that is harder to measure. (11) A teenager who watches a retired electrician open a lamp learns how it works, and the electrician is there too.

(12) The library has offered its meeting room at no charge. (13) What the program needs now is more volunteers, and anyone who can sew, solder, or simply hold a flashlight is welcome.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: a buried creek (practice text)
stimuli.text: (1) A creek once ran through the center of our town. (2) In the 1950s, it was sealed inside a concrete pipe and buried under a parking lot. (3) Several cities have recently dug up buried streams and restored them to open channels, a practice called daylighting. (4) An open stream can hold more water during storms than a pipe, so nearby streets flood less often. (5) It also gives fish and birds a place to live. (6) The town plans to repave the lot next year. (7) Before it does, it should study whether our creek could be brought back to the surface.

stimuli.title: An essay by a railroad engineer, 1884 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Not two years ago, a traveler who crossed this country by rail needed to carry a small library of timetables and a good deal of patience. Every city kept its own time, set by the sun at its own noon, so that when it was twelve o'clock in Chicago it was some minutes past twelve in Pittsburgh and some minutes short of it in St. Louis. The railroads, which had to fit these clocks together, kept more than fifty standards of their own. A man who missed his connection could not always say whose clock had cheated him.

On a single day in November of last year, the railroads put an end to this confusion. They divided the country into four great belts, each an hour apart, and set every station clock within a belt to the same hour. In most towns the change moved the hands only a few minutes. In return, the traveler gained a timetable he could read and a connection he could trust.

Not everyone has welcomed the change. Some ministers protest that the railroads have no business telling the sun when to rise, and a few towns have stubbornly kept the old time, so that their clocks now disagree with their own depots. I understand the feeling. There is something in a town's own noon that belongs to it, as its church bell belongs to it. But the sun has not been consulted for many years in any practical matter. The farmer rises by it still; the factory hand rises by the whistle.

The objection, at bottom, is not to a new time but to a new master. People suspect that a company has taken a power that ought to belong to the public, and in this they are not wholly wrong. The railroads acted because no government would. If the nation finds the new hours useful, as I believe it will, then the nation ought to adopt them by law, so that the hour belongs to all of us and not to the timetable.

Whatever the law decides, the experiment has already taught a lesson. A country this large cannot run on a thousand private clocks. It must agree, even on something as small as the minute, if its parts are to work together.

stimuli.title: A pamphlet by a country physician, 1722 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
It is now commonly said in the coffee houses that the new practice of inoculation is a tempting of Providence, and that a man who gives the smallpox to a healthy child is guilty of whatever follows. I do not doubt the sincerity of those who say it. I ask only that they hear what I have seen before they judge what they have not.

In the late visitation of the smallpox upon this town, I inoculated some scores of persons, young and old, by placing a little matter from a mild case into a small cut in the arm. Most fell sick within a week, kept their beds a few days, and rose again marked with only a handful of pocks. A very few died. Among those who took the disease in the common way, by breathing the air of the sick, the dead were counted not by ones but by the hundred, and the survivors were very often scarred or blinded.

I will not pretend the practice is without danger. It is a disease, and a disease may kill. But the question before a parent is not whether inoculation is safe. It is whether it is safer than the smallpox, which comes to nearly every family in its time and asks no one's leave. Between a small danger chosen and a great danger waited for, I cannot see that Providence requires us to choose the greater.

Some object that the operation spreads the distemper to the neighbors. This is a fair complaint, and it may be answered by keeping the inoculated apart until they are well, as we keep a ship from port until its crew is clean. It is no argument against the practice; it is an argument for doing it carefully.

I have no wish to win a quarrel. I wish to save children. If any reader can show me a safer way, I will take it up tomorrow and thank him for it. Until then, I shall go on as I have begun, and I shall keep an honest count of the living and the dead.

stimuli.title: An essay by a mountaineer, 2015 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
The summit was four hundred feet above us when I turned around. It was eleven in the morning, the sky was clear, and my partner and I had spent two years and most of our savings getting to that ridge. We had agreed, weeks before, that we would turn back at eleven wherever we were. We were slower than we had planned, and the agreement held. I have never regretted it, though I have regretted many easier decisions.

Climbers have a name for what we resisted that morning. They call it summit fever: the pull of a goal so close that every reason to stop begins to sound like an excuse. The danger is not that climbers are reckless. Most are careful people. The danger is that a plan made in the calm of base camp loses its authority as the goal comes into view, and the closer you are, the more it seems that the rules were written for someone else.

This is why the turnaround time matters more than any piece of equipment. It is a decision made in advance by a clearer mind than the one you will have at altitude. Its value lies precisely in its stubbornness. A rule that can be renegotiated on the mountain is not a rule; it is a suggestion, and the mountain is a poor place to take suggestions from yourself.

I do not want to make a virtue of timidity. Climbers who never push past their comfort reach nothing worth reaching, and some days the honest judgment is to go on. But there is a difference between a judgment and a wish. A judgment can explain itself. A wish just says "so close."

I think of that morning when I watch people chase other summits: the promotion, the deadline, the record. Every one of them has its own fever, and very few come with a turnaround time. Perhaps they should.

stimuli.title: An essay by a high school teacher, 2023 (practice text)
stimuli.text:
Every year a student tells me, in a tone of real complaint, that she is bored. I used to treat this as an emergency. I would reach for a game, a video, a new activity, anything to fill the silence before it spread. I have since come to think that boredom is not the problem I took it for, and that my rush to cure it may have been doing harm.

Consider what boredom is. It is the feeling of a mind with nothing to push against. In that discomfort, the mind starts looking for something to do, and if nothing is handed to it, it will sometimes invent something. Psychologists who have studied the state have found that people made mildly bored before a creative task often produce more ideas than people who are not. The empty minute is not empty; it is where wondering begins.

My students rarely get such minutes. A phone fills every gap between classes, and a feed is designed so that it never runs out. I do not blame them; I carry the same phone. But a habit of never being bored is also a habit of never being left alone with one's own thoughts, and I have watched students grow uneasy in even a minute of quiet.

None of this is a case for dull teaching. A lesson that bores students because it is poorly planned is simply a bad lesson. The boredom I mean is different: the pause after a hard question, the five minutes before anyone has an idea, the walk home without headphones. Those pauses can feel like nothing is happening. They are often where the most important work is done.

So I have stopped rushing. When a student tells me she is bored, I say that I believe her, and that I am curious what she will do about it. Some of them are annoyed. A surprising number come back with an idea.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: CPR before graduation (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) Last spring, a man collapsed in the bleachers during a baseball game at our school. (2) A parent who happened to be a nurse began chest compressions while someone ran for the school's defibrillator. (3) The man survived. (4) Many people in the stands said afterward that they would not have known what to do.

(5) Our school should teach every student hands-only CPR before graduation. (6) Most cardiac arrests outside hospitals happen at home or in public places, far from a doctor. (7) A person whose heart has stopped needs help within minutes, often before an ambulance can arrive. (8) Bystanders who start chest compressions right away can double or even triple a person's chance of survival.

(9) Some teachers worry that a new requirement would take time from other classes. (10) A basic lesson in hands-only CPR takes less than an hour. (11) Many states already require CPR training for graduation, and schools there fit it into health or physical education.

(12) An hour of class time is a small cost. (13) It is a thing that could matter for people.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: old lighthouses (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) For more than two centuries, keepers lived at lighthouses along the American coast. (2) They carried oil up the tower stairs, kept the lamp burning from dusk to dawn, and rang the fog bell when the coast vanished from view. (3) By the late twentieth century, automated lights had replaced nearly all of them. (4) Today many lighthouses stand empty, and some are falling apart.

(5) Coastal towns should restore their old lighthouses and open them as museums. (6) A lighthouse is a record of how people once lived and worked at the edge of the sea. (7) Keepers' logbooks describe shipwrecks, rescues, and the long, ordinary days in between. (8) A restored lighthouse would also draw visitors, who shop and eat in the town.

(9) Restoring a lighthouse is not cheap. (10) Salt air eats away at iron and stone, and repairs must be made by specialists. (11) Still, many towns have found partners. (12) Under a federal law, the government can transfer old lighthouses to local groups that agree to care for them.

(13) A lighthouse once kept ships safe. (14) Now it can keep a piece of history safe.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: protected bike lanes (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) Last year, our city painted bike lanes on six downtown streets. (2) The lanes are marked by a white stripe and a small bicycle symbol, and that is all. (3) Cars park in them, delivery trucks idle in them, and drivers drift into them while turning. (4) Many people who would like to ride to work still do not feel safe doing so.

(5) The city should replace the painted lanes with protected ones. (6) A protected lane is separated from traffic by a curb, a row of posts, or a line of parked cars. (7) Cities that have built connected networks of protected lanes have seen more people riding and fewer riders hurt. (8) Protected lanes also help drivers, who no longer have to guess where a cyclist will be.

(9) Some drivers worry that giving street space to bikes will slow car traffic. (10) Studies of streets that added protected lanes have found that car travel times changed little, partly because drivers no longer had to slow down behind cyclists. (11) A protected lane can keep traffic moving rather than clog it.

(12) Painting a stripe was a start. (13) Maybe the city could think about doing more someday.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: ghost signs (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) On the brick side of an old hardware store downtown, you can still read the faded words "Feed, Seed and Hardware," painted more than eighty years ago. (2) Sign painters call these old ads ghost signs. (3) Before printed billboards, painters climbed scaffolds and lettered them by hand, often working from memory. (4) Our town has at least a dozen.

(5) Several of them are about to disappear. (6) A developer plans to cover two walls with new panels, and others are fading a little more each winter. (7) The town should protect its ghost signs. (8) They show what our streets sold, what our grandparents read, and how a skilled trade looked before computers.

(9) Protecting a sign does not have to mean repainting it. (10) Some towns simply photograph and record each sign. (11) Others ask owners to leave a sign uncovered when they renovate. (12) A few have repainted their best signs, though critics say that turns history into decoration.

(13) Each and every one of these approaches costs a small amount that is little. (14) The signs have stayed on our walls for decades. (15) It would be a shame to lose them in a single season.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: learning music as an adult (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) At forty-three, my mother decided to learn the cello. (2) She had never read a note of music. (3) Her first months were painful to hear, and she nearly quit twice. (4) Three years later she plays in a community orchestra.

(5) Many adults believe it is too late to learn an instrument. (6) They assume that children learn music easily and adults cannot. (7) Children do have some advantages, such as more free time and teachers who make them practice. (8) But adults have advantages of their own. (9) They can choose music they love, practice with a clear goal, and they understand why a teacher asks them to repeat a passage.

(10) Learning an instrument also gives adults something that is rare in grown-up life: the experience of being a beginner. (11) Most of us spend our days doing what we already know how to do. (12) Being bad at something, and slowly getting better, is humbling and good.

(13) Adults who have always wanted to play should rent an instrument and find a teacher. (14) The first months will be hard.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: native plants (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) The American lawn covers more ground than any irrigated crop in the country. (2) It needs mowing every week, watering in dry spells, and often fertilizer and weed killer. (3) For all that work, a lawn offers very little to wildlife.

(4) Homeowners should replace part of their lawns with native plants. (5) Native plants are the ones that grew in a region before European settlement. (6) Because they are adapted to local rain and soil, most need little watering once they are established. (7) They also feed local insects, which in turn feed birds. (8) Many caterpillars can eat only a few kinds of native plants, and most songbirds raise their young on caterpillars.

(9) Some neighbors may find a native garden messy. (10) A neat border, a path, or a small sign can show that the garden is planned. (11) Starting small also helps; a single bed by the front walk is enough to begin.

(12) A yard can be more than a carpet of grass. (13) It can be a place where things live.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: the winter bird count (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) Every winter for more than a century, volunteers across North America have spent a day counting birds. (2) The count began in 1900 as an alternative to a holiday tradition of hunting as many birds as possible. (3) Today tens of thousands of people take part, from expert birders to families with a single pair of binoculars.

(4) Their tallies have become one of the longest records of wildlife in the world. (5) Scientists have used the data to show that many species now spend the winter farther north than they did decades ago. (6) No team of professional researchers could cover so much ground every year.

(7) Our science class should join this year's count. (8) Students would learn to identify birds, record data carefully, and see how their work fits into a larger study. (9) The count is free to join, and local organizers often pair beginners with people who are good at it.

(10) Some students may worry that they know too little to help. (11) But no one starts as an expert, and every careful count adds to the record. (12) This winter, we could add ours.

stimuli.title: A student's draft: fare-free buses (practice text)
stimuli.text:
(1) Two years ago, a small city a few hours north of us stopped charging fares on its buses. (2) Ridership rose by about a third within a year. (3) Drivers reported that buses ran faster, because riders no longer stopped at the front to pay. (4) Older residents and students, who are least likely to drive, rode the most.

(5) Our city should try the same experiment. (6) Fares pay for only a small share of what our bus system costs; most of the money already comes from taxes. (7) Collecting fares has costs of its own, including fare boxes, cards, and the staff who manage them. (8) Ending fares would make the buses easier to use for the people who depend on them.

(9) Some people who obviously have not thought it through argue that free buses attract riders who would otherwise walk or bike, not drivers. (10) This is a fair point, and it means that fare-free buses alone will not empty our roads. (11) But the goal is not only fewer cars. (12) It is a bus system that serves everyone who needs it.

(13) The city could start with a one-year trial on its busiest routes. (14) If it fails, the fares can return.

questions.stem: The speaker's exigence for the speech is
options: a recent loss of jobs at the city's foundry
a shortage of teachers in the city's schools
complaints about crime near the city's saloons
a proposal to spend public money on a library
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the council is "asked tonight to spend the public money on a free library," and the whole speech answers that question. The foundry and the saloons appear only as examples within the argument.

questions.stem: In the first sentence, the speaker's promise to speak briefly mainly serves to
options: criticize the council for limiting each speaker's time
summarize the argument he is about to make
win goodwill by respecting the council's wishes
show that he knows little about libraries
questions.explanation: By agreeing to honor the council's request, the speaker shows respect for his audience before asking it for money. He does not criticize the limit or summarize his case there.

questions.stem: The speaker states the objection that a library is "a luxury for the idle" in the first paragraph primarily in order to
options: answer it in the paragraphs that follow
show that he shares the council's doubts
prove that the city's workers dislike reading
suggest that the library should charge a fee
questions.explanation: Naming the objection first lets the speaker take it apart: the second paragraph shows that workers are not idle and that a free library matters most to those without money. He never agrees with it.

questions.stem: The examples of the foundry worker, the clerk and the mother in the second paragraph serve mainly as evidence that
options: the city's workers have real uses for books
the workers are better educated than the rich
the library should hold mostly technical books
most of the city's workers already own books
questions.explanation: Each example shows a busy working person who could put a book to use, which answers the claim that workers have no need of a library. Nothing suggests the workers own books or are better educated.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the claim of the second paragraph?
options: Wealthy citizens should give their books to the city
Mothers need books more than any other citizens do
A free library matters most to those who cannot buy books
Workers should be allowed to read books during working hours
questions.explanation: The paragraph builds to "It is precisely because these citizens have little time and less money that a free library is no luxury for them," sharpened by the contrast between the rich man's shelves and "ours."

questions.stem: The speaker's reasoning in the third paragraph relies mainly on
options: a personal story about a man who stopped drinking
the authority of well-known temperance leaders
an analogy that exposes a flaw in an objection
figures comparing saloons with reading rooms
questions.explanation: The speaker compares the objection to arguing that no one should be offered water because some will drink, showing that the objection proves too much. He offers no figures, authorities or personal story.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the speaker qualifies his argument by
options: admitting that the library may cost more than the council planned
conceding that reading does not guarantee good character
granting that most workers prefer the saloon to books
agreeing that the poor have little time for reading
questions.explanation: "I will not pretend that books make men good" limits the claim: the library promises opportunity, not virtue. The speaker never concedes on cost, and in the third paragraph he grants only that the saloon may draw more men.

questions.stem: The reference to "a republic that asks every man to judge the questions of the day at the ballot box" appeals chiefly to the council's
options: fear of higher city taxes
religious duty to the poor
sense of civic responsibility
pride in the city's industry
questions.explanation: Linking reading to voting presents the library as a support for self-government, an appeal to the councilmen as officials of a republic. The passage does not mention taxes, religion or civic pride in industry.

questions.stem: The sentences "The rich man has his own shelves. The poor man has only ours." are effective mainly because their
options: questions invite the council to respond
formal wording flatters wealthy listeners
humor softens the speaker's criticism
short, parallel form sharpens the contrast
questions.explanation: Two brief sentences built the same way set the rich man against the poor man, so the difference in their access to books lands hard. They are statements, not questions, and they are not humorous.

questions.stem: The speaker's tone throughout the speech is best described as
options: nostalgic and sentimental
bitter and accusatory
reasonable and persuasive
detached and technical
questions.explanation: He anticipates objections, concedes a point and argues by comparison, all while remaining courteous to the council. Nothing in the speech is bitter, nostalgic or technical.

questions.stem: The final paragraph develops the argument mainly through
options: a comparison between the library and paved streets
a warning about the dangers of doing nothing
a summary of each of the objections the speaker answered
a list of the books the library will first buy
questions.explanation: The speaker sets the library beside street paving, which the council already funds because the city needs it, and asks it to "pave one road more." He does not list books or restate the objections.

questions.stem: In the last sentence, "pave one road more" functions as
options: a literal request for a new street
a concession that streets come first
an ironic comment on muddy roads
a metaphor for funding the library
questions.explanation: Having compared the library to paved streets, the speaker uses "pave one road more" figuratively: the library is another road the city needs. He is not asking for an actual street.

questions.stem: The writer's primary purpose is to
options: explain how planners design successful public plazas
criticize residents who complain about city benches
trace the history of downtown streets and sidewalks
argue that cities should keep and add public seating
questions.explanation: The essay builds from the loss of seating to its effects, evidence and a concession, ending with "we should stop treating it as a problem to be solved." The plaza research and the complaints serve that argument.

questions.stem: The writer most likely has which audience in mind?
options: Researchers who study public plazas
General readers who walk city streets
Engineers who build public furniture
Store owners who removed their benches
questions.explanation: The opening invites "you" to walk downtown and count seats, and the examples are everyday people. The writer explains research rather than addressing researchers, and does not single out store owners.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the details about metal studs and armrests serve as evidence that
options: most benches downtown are poorly maintained
cities have made it harder to sit in public
public seating is expensive to install
downtown businesses want more customers
questions.explanation: Removed benches, studded ledges and divided seats all show that sitting in public has been made harder. Maintenance and cost come up only later, in the fourth and fifth paragraphs.

questions.stem: The second paragraph relates to the first mainly by
options: questioning the facts given in the first paragraph
giving the history of the trend just described
proposing a solution to the problem just described
showing who pays the price for the trend described
questions.explanation: After the first paragraph describes the loss of seating, the second shows its effect on older people, pregnant women, children and workers. Solutions come in the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: The sentence "When a city removes seating to discourage one kind of visitor, it discourages every kind" states
options: the claim the examples before it support
a concession to people who dislike benches
a counterargument the writer goes on to refute
a fact taken from research on public plazas
questions.explanation: The list of ordinary bench users leads to this general claim, which the writer endorses. The plaza research comes in the next paragraph and the concession in the fourth.

questions.stem: The writer supports the claim in the third paragraph mainly with
options: a memory of a crowded plaza from childhood
the cost of benches compared with other projects
interviews with people who own downtown shops
findings from research on public plazas
questions.explanation: "Researchers who filmed public plazas found" introduces the evidence: the plazas people chose had plenty of seating. There are no memories, interviews or costs in that paragraph.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, the sentence "People attract people, and seating is what keeps them long enough to attract anyone" functions as
options: a transition to the writer's concession
a definition of a planner's term
a conclusion drawn from the research
a counterargument the writer rejects
questions.explanation: The sentence explains what the plaza findings mean: seating keeps people in a place, and their presence draws others. It sums up the evidence rather than opposing it or defining a term.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer responds to opponents by
options: proposing that public seating be moved indoors
denying that any complaint about public benches is valid
arguing that most complaints come from tourists
granting a problem and offering upkeep as the answer
questions.explanation: "None of this means that complaints about benches are imaginary" grants that neglected or badly placed seating is a nuisance, then answers that the cure is "a well-managed one, not an empty sidewalk."

questions.stem: The claim that busy streets are "by most measures, safer ones" is used to suggest that
options: safety matters less than comfort downtown
well-kept seating can make a street safer
cities should count the people on streets
benches attract crime to city centers
questions.explanation: The writer links added and maintained seating to busier streets, and busier streets to safety, answering the worry that benches cause trouble. The other choices reverse or ignore that reasoning.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the word "quietly" suggests that the message to keep moving is
options: spoken softly by city officials
hidden from the people who made it
meant only for visitors to the city
sent by design rather than stated
questions.explanation: No sign tells people to move along; the missing benches and studded ledges say it for the city. "Quietly" describes that unspoken message, not a soft voice.

questions.stem: The list in the second paragraph ("A child with a sprained ankle, a delivery worker on a break, a tourist reading a map") mainly emphasizes
options: how risky city streets can be
how little the writer trusts officials
how varied a bench's users are
how crowded the sidewalks have become
questions.explanation: Placing very different people side by side, all followed by "all of them use a bench," shows how many kinds of people depend on public seating. The list is not about crowding or danger.

questions.stem: Calling a bench "the most democratic piece of furniture we have" emphasizes that benches
options: cost less than other furniture
were first built by elected officials
serve everyone on equal terms
are chosen by a public vote
questions.explanation: "Democratic" here means open to all alike: a bench "asks nothing of the person who uses it." Its low cost is stated separately in the paragraph and is not what the word conveys.

questions.stem:
In sentence 4 (reproduced below), the writer wants to state the position the essay will argue.

Results like these __say something about trees__.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
were recorded carefully by the volunteers that afternoon
show why our city should plant trees on every street
surprised many of the people who took part
questions.explanation: The rest of the draft argues for a citywide planting program, so sentence 4 should state that position. The current wording is vague, and the other choices describe the experiment instead of a claim.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 6. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it explains how shade lowers the air temperature
Keep it, because it shows why cooler streets matter for health
Delete it, because it repeats the point made in sentence 5
Delete it, because it shifts the focus away from trees
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 says shade matters most during heat waves; sentence 6 tells the reader why, since heat is the deadliest weather. Without it the stakes are unclear. It does not explain how shade works.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add evidence to support the claim in sentence 7. Which choice would best accomplish this goal?
options: Many residents enjoy the color of the leaves each fall.
Oak trees can live for more than two hundred years.
City crews clean the storm drains every spring.
A city study found fewer flooded basements on tree-lined blocks.
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 claims that trees reduce flooding, and only the study about flooded basements addresses flooding and trees together. The others are true-sounding but off the point.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 10, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects sentence 10 to sentences 8 and 9?
options: For example,
Similarly,
In addition,
However,
questions.explanation: Sentences 8 and 9 grant the residents' concern; sentence 10 answers it. "However" marks that turn. "For example" and "Similarly" would treat the answer as more of the same concern.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

The difference was no accident: dark pavement in full sun soaks up heat all afternoon.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 3
After sentence 7
After sentence 9
After sentence 12
questions.explanation: "The difference" refers to the twenty-degree gap reported in sentence 3, so the new sentence belongs right after it, explaining the result before the writer states a position.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 8 and 9 (reproduced below)?

Some residents worry that tree roots will crack sidewalks. This concern is reasonable.
options: Reasonable is the worry of residents about roots that crack sidewalks.
Some residents reasonably worry that tree roots will crack sidewalks.
Some residents worry that tree roots will crack sidewalks, it is reasonable.
Some residents, which is reasonable, worry about roots cracking sidewalks.
questions.explanation: Turning sentence 9 into the adverb "reasonably" keeps both ideas in one clear sentence. The second choice is a comma splice, "which" in the third has no clear antecedent, and the fourth is awkwardly inverted.

questions.stem:
In sentence 12 (reproduced below), the writer wants to state the benefit of the program precisely.

A citywide planting program would __help out with things for__ the people who need it most.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
bring the most relief to
make a difference, sort of, for
be a nice thing to do for
questions.explanation: "Bring the most relief to" names the benefit, relief from heat, and matches the formal register of the draft. The other versions are vague or casual.

questions.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a sentence that urges the city council to act. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The council should fund the program in next year's budget.
Some residents may not want new trees near their homes.
Many cities around the world have planted street trees.
Trees have lined city streets for hundreds of years.
questions.explanation: Only the first choice addresses the council and asks for a specific action. The others state background facts or raise a doubt, which weakens the ending.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 3 that makes the problem clear to readers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The storeroom is kept at a steady, cool temperature.
Some of the quilts were made more than a century ago.
In effect, most of the town's history is hidden from the town.
The museum also has a small gift shop by the entrance that sells postcards.
questions.explanation: The essay's problem is that most of the collection cannot be seen. The first choice states that problem and its cost to the town; the others add details that do not matter to the argument.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 6.

Quilting was a common pastime in rural communities.

Should the writer add this sentence?
options: Yes, because it supports the claim about families' research
Yes, because it explains why the museum owns so many quilts
No, because it does not support the case for putting images online
No, because it repeats information that is already given in sentence 1
questions.explanation: The paragraph lists who would benefit from online images. A fact about quilting does not support that claim, so it would distract. Sentence 1 mentions quilts but not quilting as a pastime.

questions.stem: Which choice, if added after sentence 7, would best support the claim it makes?
options: Most universities have large libraries and archives of their own, with many trained staff.
Some small museums ask visiting researchers to make an appointment several weeks in advance.
A diary in one county's online collection led a historian to correct the date of a battle.
Many researchers say they prefer to handle the original objects rather than photographs of them.
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 claims that online images could let researchers make discoveries. The diary example shows exactly that happening. The third choice works against the claim, and the others are beside the point.

questions.stem: The writer wants to begin the third paragraph with a sentence that connects it to the second. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The museum opened many years ago.
Online collections are now common.
These benefits come with real costs.
Some objects are too fragile to show.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists benefits; the third turns to costs and how to meet them. "These benefits come with real costs" links the two. The other sentences do not lead into the discussion of cost.

questions.stem:
In sentence 9 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

It takes cameras, storage, and staff __time a small__ museum may have only one paid employee.
options: (as it is now)
time, so that a small
time, a small
time, and a small
questions.explanation: Two independent clauses need a comma and a conjunction; "and" adds the second difficulty. The current text is a run-on, a comma alone is a comma splice, and "so" wrongly makes the small staff a result of the costs.

questions.stem:
In sentence 12 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text best connects it to sentence 11?

__But__ protection is only half of a museum's job.
options: (as it is now)
For instance,
In the same way,
Therefore,
questions.explanation: Sentence 11 grants that storage protects the objects; sentence 12 turns to what that leaves out. "But" signals the contrast. "Therefore" and "In the same way" would treat sentence 12 as following from or agreeing with sentence 11.

questions.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 13 so that the essay ends with an image that recalls sentence 3. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The other half is sharing, and the internet makes it easy.
The other half is sharing, and a basement shares nothing.
The other half is sharing, and museums should share more.
The other half is sharing, which matters a great deal.
questions.explanation: Returning to the basement of sentence 3 frames the essay and makes the point vivid. The other endings restate the idea in general terms without the echo.

questions.stem: The writer plans to send the draft to the museum's board of directors. Which sentence, if added after sentence 10, would best address the board's likely concern?
options: Many large museums finished this kind of work years ago.
Photographs can be taken in color or in black and white.
With such help, the project need not strain the museum's budget.
Volunteers also enjoy learning about the history of the area.
questions.explanation: A board will worry first about cost, and sentence 10 has just named grants and volunteers. The first choice draws the conclusion the board needs. The others do not speak to its concern.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 2 that shows understanding of the teachers' point of view. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: They meant well; for them, college had opened every door.
Teachers often have far too many students to advise.
My grades had always been highest in science classes.
Electricians must pass an exam before working alone.
questions.explanation: Acknowledging that the teachers acted from their own experience treats them fairly, which makes the argument more persuasive to readers who share their view. The others do not address the teachers' reasoning.

questions.stem: Which sentence most clearly states the main claim of the draft?
options: Sentence 2
Sentence 3
Sentence 4
Sentence 5
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 says what schools should do, and the sentences around it support or extend that claim. Sentence 2 gives the teachers' assumption, sentence 3 the writer's own experience and sentence 4 a supporting fact.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 4 that electricians are needed everywhere. Which evidence would best accomplish this goal?
options: The number of students who graduate from the writer's school
Data on job openings for electricians across the country
A description of the tools electricians use on the job
The names of famous people who worked in the trades
questions.explanation: A claim about demand everywhere is best supported by nationwide figures on job openings. The other evidence does not show demand.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 6, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 5?
options: Nevertheless,
In contrast,
For example,
However,
questions.explanation: Sentence 6 gives specific ways schools could present apprenticeships as an equal choice, so it illustrates sentence 5. The other transitions signal a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem:
In sentence 5 (reproduced below), the writer wants to stress the gap between how apprenticeships are seen and how they should be seen.

Schools should present apprenticeships as __an equal choice, not a fallback__.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
one option among several
a possible choice for some
a path that might be good
questions.explanation: Setting "an equal choice" against "a fallback" names both the current view and the better one. The other versions are vague and lose the contrast.

questions.stem: The speaker's primary purpose in the address is to
options: warn the graduates against careers in medicine
describe the training needed to become a physician
praise the education the graduates have received
urge the graduates to question their own judgments
questions.explanation: The story, the lesson about certainty and the closing wish all point the graduates toward admitting error. The speaker's career is the example, not the subject.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the speaker builds credibility with the audience mainly by
options: noting how many years he has practiced medicine
admitting he learned his advice by failing
listing the honors he has received
quoting respected medical textbooks
questions.explanation: Saying that his one piece of advice came from "failing to follow it" makes him seem honest rather than superior. He names no honors, years or textbooks.

questions.stem: The first paragraph prepares for the rest of the address mainly by
options: describing the setting of the graduation ceremony
contrasting what school rewards with what life rewards
posing a question that the speaker later answers
summarizing the story the speaker is about to tell
questions.explanation: School rewarded right answers; the world will reward "noticing when your answers are wrong." The rest of the address explains that contrast. The story itself is not summarized.

questions.stem: The story in the second paragraph serves mainly as evidence that
options: village schools teach practical knowledge
certainty can blind an expert to the facts
fevers are often caused by bad water
medical books of the time were unreliable
questions.explanation: The speaker was sure of his diagnosis and missed what was in front of him, which the third paragraph names directly: "The great danger is certainty." The well is a detail of the story, not its point.

questions.stem: The sentences "I had looked at his chart a hundred times. She had looked at him." suggest that the speaker had
options: ignored the farmer's chart entirely
relied on records instead of observing the patient
visited the farmer less often than his wife had done
lacked the training needed to read a chart
questions.explanation: The contrast between the chart and "him" shows that the doctor studied paper while the wife watched the patient and noticed the pattern. He had looked at the chart often, not ignored it.

questions.stem: The third paragraph functions mainly to
options: shift the focus from medicine to other fields
answer an objection raised by the graduates
draw a general lesson from the story just told
introduce a second story from the speaker's career
questions.explanation: "I tell this story ... because it holds the whole of what I know" turns the anecdote into a principle about certainty. Other fields appear only in the fourth paragraph.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, the speaker distinguishes ignorance from certainty on the grounds that
options: certainty is found mainly among the young
both can be avoided by careful reading
study cures ignorance, while certainty blinds
ignorance is the greater of the two dangers
questions.explanation: "Ignorance can be cured with study," while certainty "closes the eyes." The speaker calls certainty the greater danger, the reverse of the third choice.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the repetition of "You will be tempted" mainly serves to
options: stress the pressures the graduates will face
signal a shift to an unrelated topic
create humor through exaggeration
suggest that the speaker doubts the graduates
questions.explanation: Repeating the phrase piles up the temptations the graduates will meet, preparing for the command "Resist." It is serious, not comic, and the topic continues.

questions.stem: The one-word sentence "Resist." is effective mainly because it
options: gives a direct command after building tension
leaves the graduates' choice deliberately open
contrasts with the technical language of medicine
repeats a word the speaker used earlier
questions.explanation: After two long sentences describing temptations, a single word delivers the speaker's instruction with force. It does not repeat an earlier word or leave the choice open.

questions.stem: The speaker's claim that most of the graduates' colleagues "will not have diplomas" is supported within the passage by
options: statistics about education at the time
the example of the farmer's wife
the opinions of other physicians
the graduates' experiences in school
questions.explanation: The wife, who had "no schooling beyond the village school," proved the best colleague the doctor had that year. That example is the only support the passage gives.

questions.stem: In the final paragraph, the speaker declines to wish the graduates success in order to
options: avoid repeating what earlier speakers said
show his doubts about the value of college
suggest that most of the graduates will fail
stress that honesty about error matters more
questions.explanation: By setting aside success, "which will come or not as it pleases," the speaker makes room for the wish he values more: the courage to say "I was wrong." He does not predict failure.

questions.stem: The speaker's tone in the final paragraph is best described as
options: bitter and regretful
playful and ironic
formal and detached
warm but candid
questions.explanation: He offers a heartfelt wish while admitting that saying "I was wrong" is hard. The paragraph is neither bitter nor joking, and its direct address is not detached.

questions.stem: The writer's primary purpose is to
options: explain how newspapers check their facts before printing
criticize readers who complain about small errors
describe the daily routine of a busy newsroom
defend corrections as a sign of a careful newspaper
questions.explanation: The essay argues that admitting errors shows care and builds trust, against colleagues who thought it made the paper look careless. Fact-checking and newsroom routine are not its subject.

questions.stem: The first paragraph establishes the writer's authority mainly through
options: a survey of readers that the writer conducted
praise for the column from the writer's colleagues
the writer's long experience running the column
the awards the newspaper received over the years
questions.explanation: "For eleven years I ran the corrections column" gives the writer firsthand knowledge. Some colleagues criticized the column rather than praising it, and the surveys mentioned later were not the writer's.

questions.stem: The writer most likely mentions the colleagues' view in the first paragraph in order to
options: show that the writer once shared that view
explain why the column was rarely read
set up the view the essay argues against
suggest that the column should be shortened
questions.explanation: The colleagues thought the column made the paper look careless; the next sentence and the rest of the essay argue the opposite. The writer never shared their view.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the sentence "The reasoning is simple, though it runs against instinct" functions as
options: a transition that introduces an explanation
the central claim of the whole essay
a concession to the writer's skeptical colleagues
a summary of the evidence given so far
questions.explanation: The sentence announces that an argument is coming, and the rest of the paragraph supplies it. The central claim appears at the end of the first paragraph.

questions.stem: The writer supports the claim that "Readers are not fools" with the observation that readers
options: notice errors about places they know
read every section of the newspaper
prefer printed papers to news online
write letters disputing the paper's opinions
questions.explanation: "They notice the misspelled name of their own street" shows that readers catch errors, so hiding them does not work. The other choices are not in the passage.

questions.stem: The writer refers to surveys in the third paragraph primarily to
options: support the claim that corrections build trust
show that most readers never notice small errors
argue that online news is less accurate
suggest that corrections should be brief
questions.explanation: The surveys find that readers who see prompt corrections rate the outlet as more trustworthy, which backs the writer's position. They say nothing about online accuracy or length.

questions.stem: The phrase "the quiet fix" in the third paragraph conveys the writer's view that such changes are
options: harmless because the errors are small
efficient because they take little space
deceptive because no one announces them
rare because editors avoid making them
questions.explanation: The writer describes a story "changed overnight with no note," leaving readers to doubt themselves, which damages trust. "Quiet" stresses that the change is hidden.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer qualifies the argument by acknowledging that
options: the column made the paper look careless
a correction cannot excuse poor reporting
most readers skip the corrections column entirely
online stories should never be changed
questions.explanation: "A correction is not a substitute for getting it right" limits the defense of the column. The writer still rejects the colleagues' view that it made the paper look careless.

questions.stem: The last two sentences of the fourth paragraph develop the argument by
options: predicting the future of newspapers
introducing a new piece of evidence
conceding that hidden errors are actually rare
reframing the choice that a newsroom faces
questions.explanation: The writer replaces "perfection versus error" with "acknowledged versus hidden error," a choice in which corrections are clearly better. No evidence or prediction is offered.

questions.stem: The parallel phrases "error that is acknowledged and error that is hidden" mainly emphasize
options: the gap between print and online news
the writer's regret over past mistakes
the two real options the writer sees
how hard it is to find every error
questions.explanation: Repeating "error that is" with opposite endings shows that error is a given and only the response differs. The phrases do not express regret.

questions.stem: The anecdote in the final paragraph serves mainly to
options: show how rarely readers contact editors
introduce a new point about online news
close with a reader's view that echoes the claim
explain why the writer finally left the newspaper
questions.explanation: The reader valued the column because it told her what the paper had not known, the same point the writer has argued. The note does not explain the writer's departure.

questions.stem: The writer's attitude toward the corrections column is best described as
options: embarrassed and defensive
indifferent and resigned
amused and dismissive
proud but clear-eyed
questions.explanation: The writer calls the column "the most important" part of the paper and keeps the reader's note, yet admits some corrections were embarrassing. That mix is pride without illusions.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 3. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it explains why the old fountains were removed
Keep it, because it puts the problem in the reader's own terms
Delete it, because it is unrelated to the draft's argument
Delete it, because it repeats the point made in sentence 2
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 turns the history in sentences 1 and 2 into a present problem any reader can picture. The reasons for removal are in sentence 2, not sentence 3.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Many were installed in the early 1900s as a public health measure.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 1
After sentence 3
After sentence 8
After sentence 11
questions.explanation: "Many" refers to the fountains of a century ago in sentence 1, and the sentence continues that history before sentence 2 explains their removal. Sentences 8 to 11 are about modern fountains.

questions.stem:
In sentence 3 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

Today a person who gets thirsty in our downtown has two __choices: buy__ a drink or go without.
options: (as it is now)
choices, buy
choices; buy
choices, they are buy
questions.explanation: A colon introduces the two choices the sentence has just announced. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, a comma blurs the relationship, and "they are" after a comma creates a comma splice.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 7. Which evidence would best accomplish this goal?
options: A list of the parks where older adults most often gather
Figures on how much bottled water is now sold each year
A photograph of one of the city's old, rusty fountains
A medical study of how the sense of thirst changes with age
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 explains the risk by saying thirst weakens with age; a study of thirst and age supports that reason directly. The other evidence does not address it.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 9, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 8?
options: In contrast,
As a result,
For example,
However,
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 gives features that show modern fountains are not "rusty spouts," so it illustrates sentence 8. Nothing in it contrasts with or results from sentence 8.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 10.

Ancient Rome had hundreds of public fountains fed by its aqueducts.

Should the writer add this sentence?
options: Yes, because it explains how modern fountain water is tested
Yes, because it shows that public fountains are a proven idea
No, because it contradicts the description in sentence 8
No, because it does not support the case for new fountains here
questions.explanation: The paragraph shows that modern fountains are clean and well used. A fact about ancient Rome interrupts that point and does nothing for the proposal.

questions.stem: The writer plans to send the draft to the parks department. Which sentence, added after sentence 14, would best address the department's likely concern about upkeep?
options: Many people now carry their own refillable bottles of water wherever they go.
Drinking fountains were once made of cast iron or of carved stone in many cities.
Several neighborhood groups have offered to report any fountain that stops working.
Some of the old fountains were decorated with colorful tiles or with carvings.
questions.explanation: A parks department will worry about keeping fountains working; volunteers who report problems speak to that concern. The others are history or habits.

questions.stem: The writer wants to revise sentence 14 so that the draft ends by recalling the choice described in sentence 3. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The parks department should include them in its plans as soon as it possibly can.
The parks department should include them in all three of the parks it is renovating.
The parks department should include them and tell the public about its decision.
The parks department should include them, so no one downtown must buy a drink or go without.
questions.explanation: Echoing "buy a drink or go without" from sentence 3 frames the draft and reminds readers what the fountains would fix. The other versions only restate the request.

questions.stem: Sentences 1 and 2 serve mainly to
options: list the kinds of items the library lends
show that the library had too many visitors that day
describe the writer's own broken appliances
create curiosity before the event is explained
questions.explanation: A toaster, a lamp and jeans that came to a library but were not "there to be borrowed" make a small puzzle that sentence 3 solves, drawing the reader in. The items were not the writer's or the library's.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 6. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it explains why so many household things break
Keep it, because it shows the idea has worked in many places
Delete it, because it contradicts the figure in sentence 4
Delete it, because it shifts to the history of libraries
questions.explanation: Showing that repair cafes have spread to thousands of communities supports the proposal that the town hold one regularly. It says nothing about why things break or about libraries.

questions.stem:
In sentence 7 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

They work because many broken things need only a small __fix; a loose__ wire, a worn belt, a missing button.
options: (as it is now)
fix, and a loose
fix. A loose
fix: a loose
questions.explanation: A colon introduces the list of examples. A semicolon must join two independent clauses, "and" wrongly adds the list as another thing needed, and a period leaves the list as a fragment.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 9 that repairs keep things out of the landfill. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The volunteers brought their own tools and supplies from home.
Some of the items brought in were more than twenty years old.
The pair of jeans needed nothing more than a new button.
Together the thirty-one items weighed more than eighty pounds.
questions.explanation: The total weight of the repaired items measures what stayed out of the landfill. The age of the items and the volunteers' tools do not.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 11, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 10?
options: In conclusion,
However,
For example,
Instead,
questions.explanation: Sentence 10 says repair cafes do something harder to measure; sentence 11 gives an instance of it. "However" and "Instead" signal a contrast that is not there.

questions.stem:
In sentence 11 (reproduced below), the writer wants to show what both people gain.

A teenager who watches a retired electrician open a lamp learns how it works, __and the electrician is there too__.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
and the electrician passes on a skill that might be lost
and the electrician is also at the library that day
and the electrician has brought a lot of tools along
questions.explanation: The teenager gains knowledge; the revision gives the electrician a matching gain, the chance to pass on a skill. The other versions say only where the electrician is or what the electrician brought.

questions.stem: The writer wants to divide the second paragraph into two paragraphs. The new paragraph should begin with
options: sentence 5
sentence 6
sentence 7
sentence 8
questions.explanation: Sentences 4 and 5 report the day's results; sentences 6 and 7 turn to background on repair cafes in general. Sentence 8 already begins the third paragraph.

questions.stem: The writer plans to publish the draft in the town newsletter. Which sentence, added after sentence 13, would best appeal to readers who might attend?
options: The Netherlands now has repair cafes in many of its larger cities.
Libraries have changed a great deal over the past twenty years.
Electricians must hold a license to do paid work in most places.
Bring a broken item next time, and a volunteer will show you the fix.
questions.explanation: A newsletter reader is invited directly to come and learn. The other sentences give background that does not speak to the reader's own part.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 1 and 2 (reproduced below)?

A creek once ran through the center of our town. In the 1950s, it was sealed inside a concrete pipe and buried under a parking lot.
options: Sealed inside a concrete pipe in the 1950s, a parking lot buried the creek that once ran through the center of our town.
A creek once ran through the center of our town, and so in the 1950s it was sealed inside a concrete pipe and buried under a parking lot.
A creek once ran through the center of our town, in the 1950s it was sealed inside a concrete pipe and buried under a parking lot.
A creek once ran through the center of our town until, in the 1950s, it was sealed inside a concrete pipe and buried under a parking lot.
questions.explanation: "Until" shows that the creek ran in the open up to the time it was buried. The second choice is a comma splice, "and so" invents a cause, and the last makes the parking lot the thing that was sealed in a pipe.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 3.

The word daylighting is also used for designing buildings that let in natural light.

Should the writer add this sentence?
options: Yes, because it defines a term that readers may not have heard
Yes, because it shows how widespread the practice has become
No, because it repeats the information already given in sentence 2
No, because it does not support the argument for restoring the creek
questions.explanation: The other meaning of "daylighting" has nothing to do with streams, so it distracts from the proposal. Sentence 3 already explains what daylighting a stream means.

questions.stem: Which choice, if added after sentence 4, would best support the claim it makes?
options: Many small creeks run nearly dry during the hottest months of late summer.
Concrete pipes can last for many decades if they are carefully maintained.
Most parking lots are paved with asphalt rather than with poured concrete.
After one city restored a buried creek, nearby streets flooded far less often.
questions.explanation: Sentence 4 claims that an open stream reduces flooding; a city where flooding fell after daylighting supports it. The other facts do not concern flooding.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 7, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to the rest of the draft?
options: For example,
Therefore,
Similarly,
In contrast,
questions.explanation: The benefits in sentences 4 and 5 and the repaving in sentence 6 lead to the conclusion in sentence 7, so "Therefore" fits. Sentence 7 is not an example or a contrast.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 7 that speaks to residents who would miss the parking spaces. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: Fish often return to a stream within a few years of its being opened up.
Concrete pipes were widely used for drainage during the 1950s and 1960s.
A restored creek could run beside a smaller lot that keeps most of its spaces.
Some towns have held contests to choose names for their restored creeks.
questions.explanation: Residents who park in the lot want to know they will not lose it; a design that keeps most of the spaces answers that worry. The others do not mention parking.

questions.stem: The writer's exigence is
options: a recent train wreck blamed on a faulty station clock
public debate over the railroads' new standard time
a proposal to extend the railroads farther west
complaints from travelers about the cost of tickets
questions.explanation: The essay responds to the change "in November of last year" and to those who have not welcomed it. No wreck, expansion or ticket prices are mentioned.

questions.stem: The details in the first paragraph serve mainly as evidence that
options: most travelers preferred to go by road
cities competed to have the earliest noon
railroads were careless with their schedules
local time made travel by rail confusing
questions.explanation: Different clocks in each city, more than fifty railroad standards and missed connections all show the confusion that standard time ended. The railroads are not called careless.

questions.stem: The phrase "a small library of timetables" in the first paragraph
options: exaggerates to stress the traveler's burden
refers to the books sold in railroad stations
praises the railroads' careful records
suggests that travelers enjoyed reading
questions.explanation: No traveler carried a real library; the overstatement shows how many timetables the old system required. The tone is wry, not admiring.

questions.stem: The second paragraph relates to the first mainly by
options: describing the change that ended the problem
raising an objection to the writer's view
showing that the problem was exaggerated
giving further examples of the old confusion
questions.explanation: The first paragraph sets out the confusion of local time; the second tells how the railroads "put an end to this confusion." Objections come in the third paragraph.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, the sentence "I understand the feeling" is most likely meant to
options: admit that the writer first opposed the change
show respect for readers who oppose the change
signal that the writer is changing the subject
suggest that most opponents are ministers
