questions.explanation: Before answering the objection, the writer grants that attachment to a town's own noon is understandable, which makes opponents likelier to listen. Nothing says the writer once opposed the change.

questions.stem: The comparison of a town's noon to "its church bell" suggests that local time
options: was less exact than the railroads' time
was set by the ministers of each town
was announced by the ringing of bells
was part of a town's sense of identity
questions.explanation: Like the church bell, the town's own noon "belongs to it": a mark of local identity. The comparison is about belonging, not about how time was announced.

questions.stem: The claim that "the sun has not been consulted for many years in any practical matter" is supported by
options: the contrast between the farmer and the factory hand
the towns whose clocks disagree with their own depots
the number of standards the railroads once kept
the ministers' protest about telling the sun when to rise
questions.explanation: The factory hand already rises by the whistle, not the sun, showing that working life has long run on clock time. The ministers' protest is the view the writer answers.

questions.stem: The phrase "not to a new time but to a new master" emphasizes that
options: the railroads treat their own workers too harshly
the real dispute is about who holds authority
the new hours are difficult to learn
clocks ought to be made by the public
questions.explanation: The "not ... but" structure moves the objection from the clock to the question of power: a company, not the public, set the time. The next sentences confirm that reading.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer partly agrees with opponents that
options: the railroads ought to give up the new hours at once
a company has taken a power that belongs to the public
the new hours are less useful than the old local time
each town should be free to keep its own local time
questions.explanation: "In this they are not wholly wrong" grants the point about power, and the writer answers it by urging a law. The writer still believes the new hours are useful.

questions.stem: The fourth paragraph moves from
options: telling a story to stating its moral
praising the railroads to blaming them
listing facts to raising a question about them
explaining an objection to proposing a remedy
questions.explanation: The paragraph identifies what opponents really object to, concedes part of it, and proposes that the nation adopt the hours by law. It contains no story or list.

questions.stem: The writer's primary purpose is to
options: persuade towns to return to their own local time
defend standard time and urge a law adopting it
explain how towns once set their clocks by the sun
criticize ministers who oppose the railroads
questions.explanation: The essay praises the change, answers objections and calls for the nation to adopt the hours by law. Local solar time is described only as the problem.

questions.stem: The final paragraph functions mainly to
options: predict which towns will adopt the change
raise a new objection to standard time
draw a general lesson from the change
summarize the history of the railroads
questions.explanation: "The experiment has already taught a lesson" introduces a broader point: a large country must agree on time for its parts to work together.

questions.stem: The writer's exigence is
options: a law that has banned the practice of inoculation
a shortage of physicians during the epidemic
public claims that inoculation is morally wrong
a quarrel with a rival physician in the town
questions.explanation: The pamphlet opens with what is "commonly said in the coffee houses": that inoculation tempts Providence and makes the inoculator guilty. No law, shortage or rival is mentioned.

questions.stem: The phrase "a tempting of Providence" reflects
options: the writer's own fear of divine punishment
the legal charge later brought against the writer
the religious terms of the critics' objection
the jokes told about the new practice
questions.explanation: The critics frame inoculation as a sin against God's will, and the writer answers in the same terms in the third paragraph. He never says he fears punishment.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the writer asks critics only to "hear what I have seen" mainly to
options: invite a fair hearing before they judge
suggest that the critics are insincere
show that he refuses to discuss the matter
boast of how many patients he has seen
questions.explanation: The writer grants the critics' sincerity and asks only that they consider evidence first, a modest request meant to keep them reading.

questions.stem: The writer's main evidence in the second paragraph is
options: a comparison of deaths in two groups
the cure of a single child in the town
the opinions of learned physicians
reports from inoculators in other lands
questions.explanation: The paragraph sets the few deaths among the inoculated against deaths "by the hundred" among those who caught smallpox naturally. It cites no authorities or foreign reports.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, "counted not by ones but by the hundred" emphasizes
options: how many persons the writer inoculated
the care the writer took in keeping records
the scale of deaths from natural smallpox
how slowly the disease spread through town
questions.explanation: The contrast between "ones" and "the hundred" magnifies the toll of the disease caught in the common way, against the "very few" inoculated who died.

questions.stem: In the third paragraph, the writer concedes that
options: Providence forbids every medical risk
the critics in the coffee houses are right
smallpox reaches only a few families
inoculation itself can sometimes kill
questions.explanation: "I will not pretend the practice is without danger ... a disease may kill" admits the risk. The writer says smallpox reaches "nearly every family," the opposite of the second choice.

questions.stem: The argument of the third paragraph turns on
options: an appeal to the authority of the church and its ministers
a story about the writer's own family
recasting the question as a comparison of risks
a list of the symptoms of smallpox
questions.explanation: The writer replaces "is inoculation safe?" with "is it safer than the smallpox?" and concludes that choosing the smaller danger is reasonable.

questions.stem: The sentence "Between a small danger chosen and a great danger waited for, I cannot see that Providence requires us to choose the greater" relies chiefly on
options: an extended metaphor of a journey
a direct question addressed to the reader
a balanced contrast between two choices
an appeal to the reader's pity
questions.explanation: "A small danger chosen" and "a great danger waited for" are set in parallel, so the reader weighs them side by side. The sentence is a statement, not a question.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer answers the complaint that inoculation spreads the disease by
options: arguing that the risk is too small to matter
denying that inoculation spreads the disease
proposing that the inoculated be kept apart
blaming the spread on ships arriving in port
questions.explanation: The writer calls it "a fair complaint" and answers it by keeping the inoculated apart until they are well. He neither denies the risk nor dismisses it.

questions.stem: The comparison to keeping "a ship from port" in the fourth paragraph functions as
options: a warning against trade with other ports
evidence that smallpox arrived by sea
a familiar precedent for the proposed remedy
a concession that the disease cannot be stopped
questions.explanation: Readers already accepted holding a ship until its crew was clean, so the comparison makes keeping the inoculated apart seem ordinary and sensible.

questions.stem: The writer's intended audience is most likely
options: physicians who already perform inoculation
the owners of the town's coffee houses
ship captains held under quarantine
townspeople and parents who doubt the practice
questions.explanation: The writer answers the doubts heard in the coffee houses and frames the choice as one "before a parent," so he addresses ordinary skeptical readers.

questions.stem: The final paragraph contributes to the argument mainly by
options: summarizing the death counts given earlier
announcing that the writer will stop the practice
presenting the writer as open to correction
attacking the motives of the writer's critics
questions.explanation: Offering to adopt any safer way "tomorrow" and to keep "an honest count" shows good faith, strengthening the writer's credibility. He says he will go on as he began.

questions.stem: The writer's primary purpose is to
options: argue for setting limits before chasing a goal
describe the dangers of weather at altitude
persuade readers to take up mountain climbing
recount the history of a famous climbing route
questions.explanation: The climb illustrates the value of a turnaround time set in advance, and the last paragraph applies that lesson to other goals. Weather and history are not discussed.

questions.stem: The writer most likely opens with the decision to turn back in order to
options: boast about how hard the climb had been
ground the argument in personal experience
blame the partner for their slow progress
explain how costly expeditions can be
questions.explanation: Beginning with a real choice made four hundred feet from the summit gives the later reasoning weight. The writer does not blame the partner, and the cost is a detail.

questions.stem: The sentence "I have never regretted it, though I have regretted many easier decisions" suggests that
options: the hard choice proved to be a sound one
the writer later reached that summit
the writer regrets most past decisions
turning back was an easy thing to do
questions.explanation: Setting this decision against "many easier decisions" stresses that it was hard and that the writer still stands by it. Nothing says the writer returned to the peak.

questions.stem: The second paragraph relates to the first mainly by
options: answering an objection to the writer's choice
explaining how the partners chose the route
describing what happened on the way down
naming the force the writer resisted
questions.explanation: "Climbers have a name for what we resisted that morning" introduces summit fever and explains it. The descent and the route are not discussed.

questions.stem: In the second paragraph, the writer claims that the danger of summit fever lies in
options: equipment failing at high altitude
climbers being careless by nature
a plan losing its force as the goal nears
sudden storms close to the summit
questions.explanation: "The danger is not that climbers are reckless ... The danger is that a plan made in the calm of base camp loses its authority" states the claim directly.

questions.stem: The writer supports the claim that "the turnaround time matters more than any piece of equipment" mainly with
options: advice from a famous mountain guide
a second story from a different climb
figures on accidents near mountain summits
reasoning about decisions made in advance
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues that a rule set by a clearer mind is valuable because it cannot be renegotiated. It cites no figures, experts or other climbs.

questions.stem: The phrase "a clearer mind than the one you will have at altitude" implies that
options: experienced climbers think more clearly
planning is easier with a partner present
climbers should plan only at the summit
nearness to a goal can cloud judgment
questions.explanation: The writer contrasts the calm of base camp with the mind near the summit, where summit fever bends reasons into excuses. Planning happens before the climb, not at the top.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer qualifies the argument by acknowledging that
options: the writer once reached a summit late
turnaround times are often set far too early
sometimes the right choice is to keep going
most climbers ignore their own rules
questions.explanation: "Some days the honest judgment is to go on" admits that pushing on can be right. The writer keeps the distinction between judgment and wish.

questions.stem: The distinction between "a judgment and a wish" in the fourth paragraph serves to
options: criticize climbers who are too cautious
separate sound reasons to go on from mere desire
show that the writer regrets turning back
restate the point of the first paragraph
questions.explanation: Having admitted that going on is sometimes right, the writer needs a test: a judgment "can explain itself," while a wish only says "so close."

questions.stem: The quoted words "so close" at the end of the fourth paragraph
options: quote what the partner said on the ridge
measure the distance left to the summit
give voice to a wish that cannot explain itself
express the writer's confidence about reaching the top
questions.explanation: The two words stand for summit fever's whole argument: no reason, only nearness. They are not attributed to the partner.

questions.stem: The final paragraph broadens the essay's audience to include
options: climbers who are planning their first high expedition
people pursuing goals far from any mountain
employers who set strict deadlines for their workers
guides who lead paying groups up to famous summits
questions.explanation: "Other summits: the promotion, the deadline, the record" extends the lesson to anyone chasing a goal. Employers are not addressed.

questions.stem: The essay is organized mainly as
options: a chronology of one climb from start to finish
a list of rules for climbers, each with its own example
a problem followed by several possible solutions
an anecdote, its analysis, a concession, an extension
questions.explanation: The writer tells the story of turning back, explains summit fever and the turnaround rule, concedes that going on can be right, and applies the lesson to other goals.

questions.stem: The writer's primary purpose is to
options: explain how teachers can plan more exciting lessons
warn students about the dangers of phones
report the results of a study of boredom
argue that some boredom is good for students
questions.explanation: The writer explains a change of mind: boredom can be where ideas begin, so it should not always be cured. Phones and research are parts of that argument.

questions.stem: In the first paragraph, the admission "I used to treat this as an emergency" mainly serves to
options: explain why the writer chose to teach
show that the writer has rethought an earlier view
suggest that boredom is a medical condition
criticize the methods of other teachers
questions.explanation: The writer describes an old habit in order to reject it: "I have since come to think that boredom is not the problem I took it for." The word "emergency" is figurative.

questions.stem: The phrase "before it spread" in the first paragraph presents boredom as
options: something like a contagion
a rule the teacher set
a reward for hard work
a welcome sign of a quiet class
questions.explanation: The writer once treated boredom as if it could infect the whole class, the view the essay goes on to reject.

questions.stem: The second paragraph contributes to the argument mainly by
options: answering an objection raised by parents
listing activities that relieve boredom
defining boredom and explaining its value
describing the writer's classroom routine
questions.explanation: "Consider what boredom is" leads into a definition and the claim that the uncomfortable pause is where invention starts, supported by research.

questions.stem: The research mentioned in the second paragraph supports the claim that
options: most students are bored in school
teachers cause most student boredom
creative tasks are themselves boring
boredom can lead the mind to new ideas
questions.explanation: People made mildly bored before a creative task produced more ideas, which backs "it is where wondering begins." The research says nothing about how many students are bored.

questions.stem: The sentence "The empty minute is not empty" relies on
options: an appeal to the authority of an expert
an apparent contradiction to make a point
a comparison with the writer's own youth
a question that invites the reader to answer
questions.explanation: Calling the empty minute "not empty" seems contradictory until the reader sees that the minute is empty of activity but full of thinking. It is a statement, not a question.

questions.stem: The claim in the third paragraph that students grow uneasy in quiet is supported mainly by
options: figures on teenagers' use of phones
the findings of psychologists
interviews with the writer's fellow teachers
the writer's own observations of students
questions.explanation: "I have watched students grow uneasy in even a minute of quiet" is firsthand observation. The psychologists appear in the second paragraph, on a different point.

questions.stem: The sentence "I do not blame them; I carry the same phone" functions to
options: excuse students who use phones in class
turn the essay toward the writer's private life
include the writer in the habit described
state the main claim of the essay
questions.explanation: By admitting the same habit, the writer avoids lecturing and keeps readers on side before making the point about never being alone with one's thoughts.

questions.stem: The writer's intended audience is most likely
options: psychologists who study boredom
teachers and parents of young people
researchers who study creativity
companies that design phone apps
questions.explanation: The essay speaks from a teacher's experience about how adults should respond to a bored student. It explains the research rather than addressing researchers.

questions.stem: In the fourth paragraph, the writer limits the claim by
options: separating useful pauses from badly planned lessons
conceding that boredom harms most students
admitting that phones help many students learn
noting that some students are never bored
questions.explanation: "None of this is a case for dull teaching" sets aside boredom caused by poor planning; the boredom the writer defends is the pause before an idea.

questions.stem: The final paragraph relates to the first mainly by
options: introducing a different kind of student
giving the writer's new answer to the same complaint
repeating the student's complaint in new words
explaining why the writer used to rush to fill the silence
questions.explanation: The essay opens with the old reaction to "I'm bored" and ends with the new one: believing the student and waiting to see what she does.

questions.stem: The writer's tone in the final paragraph is best described as
options: anxious and uncertain
calm and quietly confident
nostalgic and sad
impatient and annoyed
questions.explanation: Short, plain sentences report the new approach and its results without fuss. The annoyance belongs to some students, not the writer.

questions.stem: Sentences 1 through 4 serve mainly to
options: describe the school's baseball season last spring
open with a real case that shows why the skill matters
praise the parent who happened to be at the game
explain how a defibrillator restarts a stopped heart
questions.explanation: The collapse, the rescue and the bystanders who "would not have known what to do" set up the proposal in sentence 5. The draft is not about baseball or the nurse herself.

questions.stem: Which sentence most clearly states the main claim of the draft?
options: Sentence 5
Sentence 8
Sentence 11
Sentence 12
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 says what the school should do, and the rest of the draft supports it. Sentences 8 and 11 are support, and sentence 12 answers the worry about class time.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 10, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 9?
options: However,
As a result,
For example,
Similarly,
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 states a worry and sentence 10 answers it, so the relationship is a contrast. A short lesson is not an example of the worry or a result of it.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 11. Which evidence would best accomplish this goal?
options: The number of people who attended last spring's game
A list of the health classes that the school now offers
A count of the states that require CPR training to graduate
A description of how a defibrillator is used on a patient
questions.explanation: Sentence 11 claims that many states already require the training, and a count of those states supports it directly. The other evidence is off the point.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

That is why the first few minutes matter more than anything that happens later.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 2
After sentence 7
After sentence 10
After sentence 13
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 says help is needed within minutes, before an ambulance arrives; the new sentence draws that conclusion and leads into the bystanders in sentence 8.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 2 and 3 (reproduced below)?

A parent who happened to be a nurse began chest compressions while someone ran for the school's defibrillator. The man survived.
options: Because a parent who was a nurse began compressions while someone ran for the defibrillator, the man survived.
A parent who was a nurse began compressions while someone ran for the defibrillator, but the man survived.
Beginning compressions while someone ran for the defibrillator, the man survived thanks to a parent.
A parent who was a nurse began compressions while someone ran for the defibrillator, the man survived.
questions.explanation: "Because" makes clear that the quick help led to survival. The second choice is a comma splice, "but" signals a false contrast, and the last says the man began the compressions.

questions.stem: The writer plans to send the draft to the school board. Which sentence, added after sentence 11, would best address the board's likely concern about cost?
options: Local fire departments often teach the lesson to schools for free.
Chest compressions should be about two inches deep for adults.
Many students already know how to call for an ambulance.
Baseball games draw large crowds on warm spring evenings.
questions.explanation: A school board will ask what the program costs, and free lessons from fire departments answer that. The other sentences do not touch cost at all.

questions.stem:
In sentence 13 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text best completes the thought of sentence 12 with precise, forceful wording?

__It is a thing that could matter for people.__
options: (as it is now)
The return could be measured in lives.
It might be useful in certain situations.
It is kind of a big deal for everyone.
questions.explanation: Sentence 12 calls the hour a small cost; "The return could be measured in lives" completes that cost-and-return idea with force. The other versions are vague or casual.

questions.stem: Sentence 2 mainly serves to
options: argue that the lighthouses should be museums
explain why automated lights replaced keepers
show the reader what a keeper's work involved
describe the shipwrecks recorded in logbooks
questions.explanation: Carrying oil, tending the lamp all night and ringing the fog bell make the keepers' job concrete. Automation, logbooks and the proposal come later.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Without them, ships would have had no light at all on the worst nights.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 2
After sentence 4
After sentence 8
After sentence 12
questions.explanation: "Them" must refer to the keepers, and "the worst nights" follows the long nights and fog in sentence 2. After sentence 4, "them" would point to empty lighthouses.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 7.

One log from 1886 records a keeper rowing out to save four sailors in a gale.

Should the writer add this sentence?
options: Yes, because it gives a vivid example of what the logbooks hold
Yes, because it shows that automating the lights was a real mistake
No, because it repeats the information already in sentence 2
No, because it shifts the focus away from the proposed museums
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 says logbooks describe rescues; a specific rescue shows why such records are worth displaying. It does not argue against automation.

questions.stem: Which choice, if added after sentence 8, would best support the claim it makes?
options: Many lighthouse lenses were made by skilled glassmakers in France during the nineteenth century.
In one coastal town, a restored lighthouse now draws thousands of visitors each summer.
Visitors must climb a great many narrow steps to reach the top of most towers.
Most lighthouses were built near rocky points and harbor entrances along the coast.
questions.explanation: Sentence 8 claims a restored lighthouse would draw visitors; a town where one does is direct support. The other facts are about the towers, not visitors.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 9 and 10 (reproduced below)?

Restoring a lighthouse is not cheap. Salt air eats away at iron and stone, and repairs must be made by specialists.
options: Restoring a lighthouse, which salt air eats away at, is not cheap, and specialists must make the repairs.
Not cheap is restoring a lighthouse, with salt air eating iron and stone and specialists making repairs.
Restoring a lighthouse is not cheap, since salt air eats away at iron and stone and repairs need specialists.
Restoring a lighthouse is not cheap, salt air eats away at iron and stone, and repairs must be made by specialists.
questions.explanation: "Since" shows that the salt damage and the need for specialists explain the cost. The second choice is a comma splice, and the last two are awkward and lose the logic.

questions.stem:
In sentence 11 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text best connects it to sentences 9 and 10?

__Still__, many towns have found partners.
options: (as it is now)
Likewise
For example
As a direct result
questions.explanation: Sentences 9 and 10 describe the cost; sentence 11 shows towns managing anyway. "Still" signals that turn. "As a direct result" would make the cost the reason towns found partners.

questions.stem: The writer plans to read the draft at a town meeting where many residents worry about cost. Which sentence, added after sentence 12, would best address that concern?
options: Many lighthouses were painted in bright stripes to be seen in daylight.
Groups that take over a lighthouse can apply for grants to pay for repairs.
Some keepers raised their families at the lighthouses they tended.
Ships today rely mostly on satellites rather than lights to navigate.
questions.explanation: Residents worried about cost need to hear how repairs would be paid for. Grants answer that directly; the other facts do not touch money at all.

questions.stem: In sentences 13 and 14, the writer mainly uses
options: a question addressed to the reader
parallel sentences that echo each other
a statistic about visitors to the town
a quotation from a former keeper
questions.explanation: "A lighthouse once kept ships safe. Now it can keep a piece of history safe." repeats the same shape, turning the lighthouse's old job into its new one.

questions.stem: Sentences 2 and 3 serve mainly to
options: describe the process of painting a bike lane
argue that drivers who park in lanes should be fined
explain why the city chose these six streets
show why the painted lanes fail to protect riders
questions.explanation: A stripe and a symbol are "all" there is, and cars, trucks and turning drivers end up in the lane. That sets up the claim that riders do not feel safe.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 4. Which evidence would best accomplish this goal?
options: A city survey in which many residents said they would ride if lanes felt safer
The total number of miles of road that the city maintains each year
A map showing the six downtown streets where the lanes have been painted
A list of the bike shops that have opened in the downtown area recently
questions.explanation: Sentence 4 is about people who would ride but feel unsafe; a survey of residents' reasons speaks to it directly. A map or list of shops does not.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 4 that appeals to readers who do not ride bikes. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: Bike shops in our city have reported a busy season.
Every rider who feels safe enough to bike is one less car in traffic.
Riding a bike is good exercise for people of every age.
Bicycles were first sold in large numbers in the United States in the 1890s.
questions.explanation: Drivers benefit when more people bike, because traffic thins. The other sentences offer history or benefits to riders, which give non-riders no reason to care.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Posts cost far less than a curb and can be installed in a single day.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 2
After sentence 6
After sentence 10
After sentence 13
questions.explanation: Sentence 6 names posts and curbs as ways to separate a lane, so a comparison of the two belongs right after it.

questions.stem:
In sentence 8 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

Protected lanes also help __drivers, who__ no longer have to guess where a cyclist will be.
options: (as it is now)
drivers; who
drivers. Who
drivers who
questions.explanation: The comma makes "who no longer have to guess" describe all drivers. Without it, the clause would limit the help to some drivers; the semicolon and period leave a fragment.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 10. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it explains how a protected lane is actually built
Keep it, because it gives evidence against the drivers' worry
Delete it, because it contradicts the claim in sentence 11
Delete it, because it repeats the point of sentence 7
questions.explanation: Sentence 10 is the evidence that lets sentence 11 answer the drivers. Without it, the reply in sentence 11 would be an unsupported assertion.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 11, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 10?
options: Thus,
In contrast,
For instance,
Meanwhile,
questions.explanation: Sentence 11 draws a conclusion from the studies in sentence 10, so "Thus" fits. It is not an example of sentence 10 or a contrast with it.

questions.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 13 with a firm call to action that completes the thought of sentence 12. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: Some people think the city could do more.
The city might consider changes later.
Perhaps more could be done in time.
Now the city should finish the job.
questions.explanation: "Finish the job" completes "a start" in sentence 12 and states the demand directly. The other versions hedge, which weakens the ending.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 1 that would help readers who have never noticed such signs. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: Most people walk past it every day without looking up.
Feed and seed were once sold to many local farmers.
Brick was a common building material in those days.
The hardware store closed its doors many years ago.
questions.explanation: Telling readers that most people never look up explains why they may not have noticed the signs, and invites them to look. The other facts do not help a reader see the signs.

questions.stem: Which sentence most clearly states the main claim of the draft?
options: Sentence 7
Sentence 8
Sentence 9
Sentence 13
questions.explanation: Sentence 7, "The town should protect its ghost signs," is the position the rest of the draft supports. Sentence 8 gives a reason for it, sentence 9 discusses the means and sentence 13 the cost.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

The two walls face the main street, where every visitor sees them.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 2
After sentence 6
After sentence 10
After sentence 14
questions.explanation: "The two walls" refers to the walls the developer plans to cover in sentence 6, and the sentence adds to the loss. Nowhere else are two walls mentioned.

questions.stem: Which choice, if added after sentence 8, would best support the claim it makes?
options: Modern signs are usually printed on large vinyl sheets and bolted onto the wall.
Most of the older buildings downtown are made of red brick.
One sign still advertises a cough remedy once sold in every local drugstore.
Sign painting is still taught at a small number of art schools.
questions.explanation: Sentence 8 says the signs show what the streets sold and what people read. A sign for a once-common product is an example. The other facts are not about what the signs reveal.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 10, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 9?
options: Similarly,
However,
As a result,
For example,
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 says protection need not mean repainting; sentence 10 gives one such way. "For example" fits. Nothing in sentence 10 contrasts with or follows from sentence 9.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 10 and 11 (reproduced below)?

Some towns simply photograph and record each sign. Others ask owners to leave a sign uncovered when they renovate.
options: Some towns simply photograph and record each sign, while others ask owners to leave signs uncovered during renovation.
Some towns simply photograph and record each sign, others ask owners to leave a sign uncovered when they renovate.
Photographing and recording each and every sign, other towns ask owners to leave a sign uncovered when they renovate.
Some towns simply photograph and record each sign, so others ask owners to leave a sign uncovered when they renovate.
questions.explanation: "While" joins the two approaches as alternatives. The second choice is a comma splice, "so" invents a cause, and the last attaches the photographing to the wrong towns.

questions.stem: The writer most likely includes the critics' view in sentence 12 in order to
options: explain how a faded sign is repainted
suggest that critics oppose any protection
show fairness by noting a drawback of one approach
argue that no sign should ever be repainted for any reason
questions.explanation: Mentioning the objection to repainting shows the writer has weighed the options, which strengthens trust. The writer does not reject repainting outright.

questions.stem:
Which version of sentence 13 (reproduced below) is most concise?

__Each and every one of these approaches costs a small amount that is little.__
options: (as it is now)
Each and every approach costs a small, little amount.
Every one of these approaches, each of them, costs little.
Each of these approaches costs little.
questions.explanation: "Each of these approaches costs little" says the same thing without the doubled words. The other versions keep the repetition.

questions.stem: The story in sentences 1 through 4 mainly serves to
options: give a real case that challenges a common belief
describe how community orchestras choose players
explain why the writer's mother nearly quit twice
show that the cello is easier than other instruments
questions.explanation: A woman who started at forty-three and now plays in an orchestra contradicts the belief, stated in sentence 5, that adults are too old to learn.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

She practiced for twenty minutes every morning before work.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 1
After sentence 3
After sentence 9
After sentence 13
questions.explanation: The new sentence explains how the mother got past the hard first months to the orchestra, so it belongs between sentences 3 and 4. After sentence 1 it would come before she had begun.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 7, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentences 6 and 8?
options: In addition,
Admittedly,
Therefore,
For example,
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 grants a point to the other side before sentence 8 answers it with "But." "Admittedly" signals that concession; "Therefore" would make it a conclusion.

questions.stem:
In sentence 9 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

They can choose music they love, practice with a clear goal, __and they understand__ why a teacher asks them to repeat a passage.
options: (as it is now)
and understanding
and understand
and to understand
questions.explanation: The list should keep one form after "can": choose, practice and understand. Each other version breaks the parallel structure.

questions.stem:
The writer is considering adding the following sentence after sentence 9.

Studies of adult learners suggest that steady practice matters more than age.

Should the writer add this sentence?
options: Yes, because it explains how an adult should choose a teacher
Yes, because it supports the claim that adults can learn well
No, because it contradicts the point made in sentence 7
No, because it repeats the belief stated in sentence 6
questions.explanation: The paragraph argues against the belief that adults cannot learn music; research on adult learners backs that argument. It does not contradict the admission in sentence 7.

questions.stem:
In sentence 12 (reproduced below), the writer wants to state the point of the third paragraph more precisely.

Being bad at something, and slowly getting better, __is humbling and good__.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
teaches a patience that adults rarely practice
is something that everyone has done at some point
is not something that most people enjoy
questions.explanation: The paragraph says being a beginner is rare in adult life; "a patience that adults rarely practice" names the specific benefit. "Humbling and good" is vague.

questions.stem:
In sentence 3 (reproduced below), the writer wants to describe the first months honestly while keeping an affectionate tone.

Her first months were __painful to hear__, and she nearly quit twice.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
a source of severe distress
objectively terrible music
unbearable for the neighbors
questions.explanation: "Painful to hear" is honest but light, fitting a daughter's fond story. The other versions are harsh or clinical and work against the draft's warmth.

questions.stem: The writer wants to replace sentence 14 with an ending that encourages hesitant readers. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: The first months will be hard for nearly every new beginner.
The first months will be hard, but my mother would tell you they pass.
The first months will be hard, so plan your time very carefully.
The first months will be hard, and many people end up quitting.
questions.explanation: Returning to the mother's story reassures readers that the hard start ends. The second choice discourages them, and the others add no encouragement.

questions.stem: Which evidence, if added after sentence 3, would best support the claim it makes?
options: A history of how lawns became popular in American suburbs after World War II
A report that many homeowners now hire a service to mow and water their lawns
A tip that grass stays green longer through the summer when it is mowed a little high
A survey of yards that found far fewer kinds of insects in lawns than in planted beds
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 claims that a lawn offers little to wildlife; comparing insect life in lawns and planted beds tests exactly that. The others are about lawn care or history.

questions.stem:
In sentence 4 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text best states a claim that the rest of the draft supports?

Homeowners should __replace part of their lawns with native plants__.
options: (as it is now)
hire gardeners to care for their yards
plant more flowers of every kind
stop mowing their lawns altogether
questions.explanation: The draft defines native plants, explains their benefits and suggests starting with one bed, all supporting the claim as written. The other versions are not what the draft argues.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 5. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it defines a term readers may not know
Keep it, because it explains why lawns need so much water
Delete it, because it contradicts the point of sentence 6
Delete it, because it repeats the claim made in sentence 4
questions.explanation: Many readers will not know exactly what "native plants" means, and the argument depends on it. Sentence 5 is a definition, not a repetition of the claim.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Oak trees can support hundreds of kinds of caterpillars.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 3
After sentence 5
After sentence 8
After sentence 13
questions.explanation: Sentence 8 explains that caterpillars depend on native plants and birds depend on caterpillars; a native tree that feeds hundreds of kinds of caterpillars extends that point.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 10, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 9?
options: As a result,
For example,
Similarly,
However,
questions.explanation: Sentence 9 states a worry and sentence 10 answers it, so the relationship is a contrast. A neat border is not an example of a messy garden.

questions.stem:
In sentence 11 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most clear?

Starting small also __helps; a__ single bed by the front walk is enough to begin.
options: (as it is now)
helps; and a
helps, a
helps a
questions.explanation: A semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses. A comma alone makes a comma splice, no punctuation makes a run-on, and "; and" doubles the connector.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 11 that speaks to readers who have little time for gardening. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: Garden centers sell many kinds of grass seed for different yards.
Native plants come in a wide range of colors, shapes and heights for any yard.
Some native plants do not bloom until the very end of summer.
Once planted, a native bed needs less care than the grass it replaces.
questions.explanation: Busy readers want to know the work involved, and a native bed needing less care than grass answers that. The others give no reason to try.

questions.stem: Sentences 12 and 13 conclude the draft mainly by
options: asking the reader a direct question
contrasting a lifeless image with a living one
repeating the statistic that opens the whole draft
quoting an expert on native gardens
questions.explanation: "A carpet of grass" suggests something flat and dead, set against "a place where things live." There is no question, statistic or quotation.

questions.stem: Sentence 2 mainly serves to
options: show that fewer people join the count today
explain how the count began as a break from hunting
describe the methods that volunteers use to count birds
argue that hunting birds should now be banned
questions.explanation: The sentence tells how the count began, as a replacement for a tradition of shooting as many birds as possible. Sentence 3 says participation has grown, not shrunk.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 4, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentences 1 through 3?
options: Nevertheless,
In contrast,
Over time,
For example,
questions.explanation: The tallies became a long record because counts piled up year after year. "Over time" signals that. Nothing in sentence 4 contrasts with sentence 3.

questions.stem: The writer is considering deleting sentence 5. Should the writer keep or delete this sentence?
options: Keep it, because it shows how scientists have used the data
Keep it, because it explains how to tell similar birds apart
Delete it, because it shifts the focus away from the class
Delete it, because it contradicts the claim in sentence 4
questions.explanation: Sentence 5 shows that the counts have real scientific value, which supports the case for joining. It is about the data, not bird identification.

questions.stem: The writer plans to give the proposal to the science teacher. Which sentence, added after sentence 8, would best appeal to that reader?
options: Some birds are easier to spot in winter than summer.
My uncle has watched birds since he was a child.
The count also fits our unit on ecosystems and data.
Binoculars are sold in many sizes and strengths.
questions.explanation: A teacher will want to know how the activity fits the course. The other sentences give background that does not bear on the teacher's decision.

questions.stem:
In sentence 9 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text is most precise and best suits the draft's tone?

The count is free to join, and local organizers often pair beginners with __people who are good at it__.
options: (as it is now)
folks who know their stuff
individuals possessing ornithological expertise
experienced birders
questions.explanation: "Experienced birders" is exact and matches the draft's plain style. The current wording is vague, the third is slangy and the fourth is needlessly formal.

questions.stem:
In sentence 11 (reproduced below), which version of the underlined text best answers the worry stated in sentence 10?

But no one starts as an expert, and __every careful count adds to the record__.
options: (as it is now)
the count is held only once each winter
many of the counts are made by experts
some birds are very hard to tell apart
questions.explanation: Students worry they know too little to help; saying that every careful count adds to the record answers that directly. The other versions add to the worry or change the subject.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Last year, a beginner on one team spotted a species not seen in the area in decades.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 3
After sentence 5
After sentence 8
After sentence 11
questions.explanation: The beginner's find is evidence that "every careful count adds to the record," so it belongs after sentence 11, before the closing invitation.

questions.stem: The writer ends the draft with the short sentence 12 mainly to
options: introduce a new argument
make a direct, hopeful appeal
summarize the count's history
admit a weakness in the plan
questions.explanation: After answering the students' worry, the brief "This winter, we could add ours" invites the class to act, echoing "adds to the record."

questions.stem: Sentence 1 mainly serves to
options: introduce a real case that the proposal builds on
describe how bus fares are collected
explain why the writer rides the bus to school each day
criticize another city's bus system
questions.explanation: The other city's experiment supplies the evidence in sentences 2 to 4 and the model for "the same experiment" in sentence 5. The writer praises it rather than criticizing it.

questions.stem:
The writer wants to add the following sentence to the draft.

Every stop where a rider fumbles for change adds seconds to the trip.

Where would the sentence best be placed?
options: After sentence 3
After sentence 6
After sentence 10
After sentence 13
questions.explanation: Sentence 3 says buses ran faster because riders no longer paid at the front; the new sentence explains why. Elsewhere it would interrupt a different point.

questions.stem: The writer wants to support the claim in sentence 6. Which evidence would best accomplish this goal?
options: A breakdown of the bus budget showing the share paid by fares
A photograph of a crowded city bus during the morning rush hour
A driver's comments about how the weather affects service
A list of every bus route in the city with its schedule
questions.explanation: Sentence 6 is a claim about how much of the system's cost fares cover, and a budget breakdown shows that share. The others do not concern funding.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a word or phrase at the beginning of sentence 7, adjusting the capitalization as needed. Which choice best connects it to sentence 6?
options: Moreover,
However,
For instance,
Instead,
questions.explanation: Sentence 7 adds a second financial reason to sentence 6, so "Moreover" fits. Nothing in it contrasts with sentence 6 or illustrates it.

questions.stem:
In sentence 9 (reproduced below), the writer wants to refer to opponents in a way that fits the fair tone of sentence 10.

__Some people who obviously have not thought it through__ argue that free buses attract riders who would otherwise walk or bike, not drivers.

Which version of the underlined text best accomplishes this goal?
options: (as it is now)
People who hate buses
Clueless opponents
Critics
questions.explanation: Sentence 10 calls the objection "a fair point," so the opponents should be named neutrally. The other versions insult them and undercut the concession.

questions.stem: Sentence 10 contributes to the argument mainly by
options: introducing new figures on ridership
rejecting the critics' point entirely
conceding a limit while keeping the main claim
shrinking the proposal to a single route
questions.explanation: The writer grants that free buses will not empty the roads but goes on, in sentences 11 and 12, to argue that the goal is broader. The point is accepted, not rejected.

questions.stem:
Which choice most effectively combines sentences 11 and 12 (reproduced below)?

But the goal is not only fewer cars. It is a bus system that serves everyone who needs it.
options: But the goal is not only fewer cars; it is a bus system that serves everyone who needs it.
But fewer cars, which is not the only goal, and a bus system serving everyone who needs it.
But the goal, not only fewer cars, is a bus system that serves everyone who needs it.
But the goal is not only fewer cars, it is a bus system that serves everyone who needs it.
questions.explanation: A semicolon joins the two related clauses and keeps the contrast clear. The second choice is a comma splice, the third changes the meaning, and the fourth is a fragment.

questions.stem: The writer wants to add a sentence after sentence 14 that reassures readers who doubt the plan. Which choice best accomplishes this goal?
options: If it works, the city will have learned something worth knowing.
Fares were first collected on streetcars more than a century ago.
Bus drivers must hold a special license to carry passengers.
Many cities have painted their buses in bright, bold colors.
questions.explanation: Pairing the worst case (fares return) with the best case (a lesson learned) shows the trial carries little risk. The other sentences do not speak to doubters.
